title: 1. Overlapping lines
scenario: US puts 10% on India and 25% on autos from everyone (2025 data)
steps: US imports from India: $107.59bn, of which vehicles (ch. 87) $2.49bn.
Most specific line wins, so Indian vehicles pay 25% and everything else from India pays 10%.
India's GDP 2025: $3,956.07bn, so exposed exports = $107.59bn ÷ $3,956.07bn = 2.72% of GDP.
Total exports hit = all US vehicle imports $337.95bn + India's non-vehicle exports $105.10bn = $443.05bn.

Today vs. scenario: the India line is country-wide, so it replaces today's 10% forced-labour duty but keeps Section 232 tariffs. Indian steel articles (ch. 73, $2.93bn) keep their 50% ($1.46bn) and add the scenario's 10%, giving $1.76bn.

title: 2. Today vs. scenario
scenario: 25% on vehicles from Mexico, replacing today's duties (2025 data)
steps: US vehicle imports from Mexico: $124.20bn. Exports hit = $124.20bn; tariff bill = 25% × that = $31.05bn.
Today USMCA vehicles pay 25% on non-US content only, modelled as 76% coverage (≈19% effective): $124.20bn × 0.76 × 25% = $23.60bn.
Average rate on the flow: today 19.0%, scenario 25.0%. Price-based change = (25.0% − 19.0%) ÷ (1 + 19.0%) = 5.04%.

title: 3. Who gains
scenario: 10% on electronics (ch. 85) from China and Vietnam (2025 data)
steps: All other suppliers sold the US $367.61bn of chapter 85.
Mexico sold $91.35bn, a 24.8% share of untaxed supply, so its diversion potential = $145.95bn × 24.8% = $36.27bn.
Diversion potentials across all untaxed suppliers add up to the value hit: it splits the hit trade, it does not create more.
